parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: coulomb as SI unit of charge
hints: Hint 1: Start from what you can measure directly - current and time. How is charge linked to current multiplied by time?
parts.proper_answer: 1 coulomb is the charge that passes a point when a current of $1\text{ A}$ flows for $1\text{ s}$ ($1\text{ C} = 1\text{ A s}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link charge to current and time**
Think of current as the rate of flow of charge. You cannot count coulombs directly, but you can measure current in amperes and time in seconds. The defining equation is $$Q = It$$ where $Q$ is charge, $I$ is current and $t$ is time.

Step 2: **Put in 1 ampere for 1 second**
If $I = 1\text{ A}$ and $t = 1\text{ s}$, then $$Q = 1 \times 1 = 1\text{ C}$$ So the coulomb is defined as the charge transferred by 1 ampere in 1 second.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Remember that all free charges come in whole multiples of one smallest amount - the elementary charge $e \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$. Which of the listed values can be made by multiplying this by a whole number?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use quantisation of charge**
Charge cannot take any value. Any isolated charge carrier must have charge $$q = \pm ne$$ where $n = 1, 2, 3...$ and $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ is the elementary charge.

Step 2: **Test each value**
$8.0 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C} = 5e$ - possible. $1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C} = 1e$ - possible. $4.0 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C} = 2.5e$ - not a whole multiple, impossible. $1.6 \times 10^{-20}\text{ C} = 0.1e$ - smaller than $e$, impossible. So only the first and third values are allowed.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: The same current $I$ must pass every cross-section. From $I = nAvq$, with $n$ and $q$ constant for the same wire, how must average drift speed $v$ change when cross-sectional area $A$ gets larger?
Hint 2: Compare the areas at S and T using $A = \pi d^2/4$. If diameter doubles, what happens to area and therefore to drift speed? Think about whether the fall is linear or curved.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at $1.00v_{s}$ at S and ending at $0.25v_{s}$ at T, falling steeply at first then less steeply - concave upwards, proportional to $1/(diameter)^2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Keep current constant**
The wire is in series with itself, so current $I$ is the same at S and at T. For free electrons: $$I = nAvq$$ where $n$ is number density, $A$ is cross-sectional area, $v$ is average drift speed and $q$ is electron charge. $n$ and $q$ do not change along the wire, so $$v \propto \frac{1}{A}$$ Larger area means slower drift to carry the same current.

Step 2: **Find the speed at T**
Area of a circle is proportional to (diameter)$^2$: $$A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}$$ At S diameter $= d$, at T diameter $= 2d$, so $$\frac{A_T}{A_S} = \frac{(2d)^2}{d^2} = 4$$ Area is 4 times larger, so drift speed is 4 times smaller: $$v_T = \frac{v_S}{4} = 0.25v_S$$

Step 3: **Get the shape correct**
Diameter increases linearly with position, but $v \propto 1/A \propto 1/d^2$. This is an inverse-square, not a straight line. So draw a smooth falling curve from $(S, 1.00v_S)$ to $(T, 0.25v_S)$ that is steep near S and flattens toward T - concave upwards with decreasing magnitude of gradient.
